Sorted epithelial cells from a donor can then be injected into that cleared space, where they will grow a new gland or a tumor. Because you choose which purified cell population goes in, any tumor that comes out must have started from that population, which turns a correlation between a cell type and a tumor into a direct test of origin.
key_methods.how_used: Basal cells (CD45 negative, EpCAM intermediate, CD49f high) and luminal cells (CD45 negative, EpCAM high, CD49f intermediate) were sorted from 4-month-old Wap-Cre mutant donors that had no overt tumor. For each implant 12,500 sorted epithelial cells were mixed with 12,500 stromal cells from the same donors in 20 microlitres of a one to one phosphate-buffered saline and growth-factor-reduced Matrigel mixture, and injected into cleared number 4 mammary fat pads of 4 to 5 week old female NSG mice. Eight recipients received basal on one side and luminal on the other, one received basal bilaterally, across two independent experiments with distinct donor pools, and tumors were collected when the largest reached 25 mm.
key_methods.why_it_matters: This is the only comparison in the paper that isolates cell of origin while holding everything else constant, since the two fractions come from the same donors and carry identical Brca1 and p53 alleles. The authors explicitly contrast it with the Wap-Cre versus Blg-Cre comparison, which confounds cell of origin with a different Cre driver and different floxed alleles. The caveats are that NSG recipients have essentially no adaptive or natural killer immunity, and that the sample size leaves tumor incidence statistically indistinguishable between the two fractions.

key_methods.name: TNBC molecular subtype classification applied across species
key_methods.plain_explanation: Triple-negative breast cancers were divided into four transcriptional subtypes by comparing each tumor's expression profile against a reference average, or centroid, for each subtype, and assigning whichever subtype it correlates with best. To apply this human classifier to mouse tumors you first have to collapse single-cell data back into one pseudo-bulk profile per animal by summing counts across its cells, then translate mouse gene names into their human equivalents.
key_methods.how_used: The web-based Vanderbilt TNBCtype classifier was used with TMM normalization. Mouse pseudo-bulk profiles were built per mouse and mapped to human genes through the MGI Homology Suite. Samples called immunomodulatory, mesenchymal stem-like or unspecified were reassigned to the highest positive centroid among BL1, BL2, LAR and M, and were called unclassified if no centroid correlation was positive. The same classifier was applied to individual cells to measure heterogeneity inside tumors, and a human mesenchymal signature was derived from TCGA basal-like TNBC and scored in the clinical cohorts with module scoring against 100 random control genes, compared by one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests.
key_methods.why_it_matters: It is the bridge between a mouse differentiation phenotype and a human clinical category, and it is what turns the observation into a translational claim. The authors themselves flag two caveats: because the classifier chose which tumors contributed to the mouse signature, the signature analysis supports the assignments rather than testing them independently, and bulk classification is sensitive to how much stroma is in a sample whereas single-cell subtyping is not, so tumors should be judged against the baseline distribution of their own dataset.

key_methods.name: CODEX multiplexed spatial proteomics (PhenoCycler)
key_methods.plain_explanation: Ordinary immunofluorescence can only show a handful of proteins at once because the fluorescent colors overlap. CODEX gets around this by attaching a short DNA barcode to each antibody, staining the tissue with the whole antibody panel at once, and then revealing the markers a few at a time across many cycles of imaging, washing and re-probing. The images are stacked so that every cell in the intact tissue has a measurement for every marker in the panel, which keeps the spatial arrangement that single-cell sequencing destroys.
key_methods.how_used: Run on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded wild-type glands, mutant glands and small and large tumors, sectioned at 5 micrometres onto poly-L-lysine coverslips, imaged on a PhenoCycler-Open system with a Keyence BZ-X800 microscope and a 20X 0.75 NA objective, and processed with CODEX Processor v1.8. Basal cells were defined as KRT14 positive, smooth muscle actin positive and KRT8 negative, luminal cells as KRT14 negative, smooth muscle actin negative and KRT8 positive, and proliferation was read from MKI67.
key_methods.why_it_matters: It places the abnormal cell state in tissue architecture, showing that basal cells lacking smooth muscle actin and the bulk of proliferation both sit in the hyperbranched hyperplastic regions of mutant glands while other regions look normal. The authors state the panel's key limitation themselves: it cannot distinguish a genuinely developmental fetal basal cell from a basal-myoepithelial cell that has simply lost its myoepithelial markers.

key_methods.name: Cross-species and developmental atlas integration (scVI and scANVI)
key_methods.plain_explanation: When single-cell datasets come from different experiments, species or technologies, the technical differences between them can be larger than the biological differences you care about. Variational autoencoder methods such as scVI learn a compressed representation of the data in which the batch or dataset of origin is explicitly regressed out, so cells of the same biological type from different sources land in the same place. The related scANVI additionally uses the labels that already exist in a well annotated reference dataset to transfer those labels onto unlabeled cells. The practical payoff is that a mouse tumor cell can be asked which annotated human or fetal cell state it most resembles.
key_methods.how_used: A public mouse mammary developmental atlas (GEO GSE164017), covering fetal, pubertal, adult, gestation, lactation and involution stages plus fetal skin, pubertal ducts and terminal end buds, was re-annotated with the same pipeline, batch corrected with scVI on sample identity using 838 highly variable genes, and used with scANVI for label transfer. The Human Breast Cell Atlas (GEO GSE235326) was reprocessed keeping its original labels, luminal hormone-sensing cells were excluded from the cross-species analysis, and mouse and human cells were co-embedded and co-clustered with Leiden, each co-cluster taking the dominant reference label.
key_methods.why_it_matters: This is how the paper argues that the abnormal basal cells resemble a fetal basal state rather than a gestational or lactational one, and how it nominates human basal-myoepithelial and LumSec-myo cells as the likely human counterparts of the Wap-Cre cell of origin. The authors are careful that this is a resemblance argument: mouse and human epithelial states correspond only weakly, and settling the human counterpart would need human lineage tracing, which they say is not currently feasible.

key_concepts.plain_definition: The cell of origin of a tumor is the specific normal cell type in which the first transforming events occurred and from which the tumor's entire cell population descends. It is a historical statement about where the cancer started. Establishing it requires either lineage tracing, where a heritable mark is placed in a defined normal cell type and later found in the tumor, or transplantation, where a purified normal population is placed somewhere it can grow and is seen to produce the tumor. Correlating a tumor's gene expression with a normal cell type is not sufficient, which is the central methodological point of this paper.

The differentiation state of a cell is the identity it is currently expressing, read out from which genes it has switched on, and it can change without the cell's ancestry changing. A tumor cell can therefore look like one cell type while having descended from another. This distinction carries the whole argument here, because the authors show that basal-myoepithelial cells lose their myoepithelial markers (ACTA2, TAGLN, MYLK) as they transform, so a tumor cell with a basal-myoepithelial origin no longer looks like a mature basal-myoepithelial cell and cannot be recognized by those markers alone.

The mammary epithelium is a bilayer. The basal-myoepithelial layer is the outer layer, sitting against the basement membrane, and its cells are contractile: they squeeze milk out of the gland during lactation. They are marked by the basal keratins KRT5 and KRT14 and the transcription factor TP63, and by the contractile proteins smooth muscle actin (ACTA2), transgelin (TAGLN) and myosin light chain kinase (MYLK). This paper's claim is that this compartment, not only the luminal one, can be the starting point of BRCA1-associated TNBC.

key_concepts.term: Secretory luminal cell and luminal progenitor (LumSec)
key_concepts.plain_definition: The luminal layer is the inner layer of the mammary bilayer, facing the duct space, and it splits into two kinds. Hormone-sensing luminal cells (LumHS) carry the estrogen and progesterone receptors (ESR1 and PGR) and respond to circulating hormones. Secretory luminal cells, also called luminal progenitors, do not carry those receptors, are marked by KIT and in mouse by Wfdc18, and are the cells that make milk proteins during lactation. These are the cells that the standard model, built on the Blg-Cre mouse and on human carrier tissue studies, holds to be the origin of BRCA1 triple-negative breast cancer.

key_concepts.term: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and its four molecular subtypes
key_concepts.plain_definition: A breast cancer is called triple-negative when it lacks the estrogen receptor, the progesterone receptor and HER2 amplification, which removes the three main targeted treatment options. It presents at a younger age, is more often metastatic at diagnosis and relapses more often. Transcriptome profiling splits it further into four subtypes: basal-like 1 (BL1), which is proliferation-driven; basal-like 2 (BL2); mesenchymal (M), which is associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, stem-like programs and distant metastasis; and luminal androgen receptor (LAR). These subtypes differ in prognosis and in response to drugs, but what decides which one a tumor becomes was unknown, and this paper proposes that the answer is the cell it started in.

key_concepts.term: Cre-loxP conditional deletion and driver specificity
key_concepts.plain_definition: To delete a gene only in certain cells, two loxP DNA sequences are placed around the part of the gene to be removed, and the enzyme Cre recombinase is expressed from a promoter that is active only in the cell type of interest. Cre cuts between the loxP sites and the intervening DNA is lost. The whole logic depends on the promoter being faithful to one cell type, and that assumption is often not checked. Here the Wap promoter is normally considered specific to secretory luminal cells, which is why the authors expected a luminal origin, but their single-cell genotyping shows recombination in basal-myoepithelial cells too.

key_concepts.term: Aneuploidy as the marker of a transformed cell
key_concepts.plain_definition: Aneuploidy means a cell carries an abnormal amount of chromosomal material, with whole chromosome arms gained or lost. It is a near-universal consequence of losing BRCA1, because the cell is forced into error-prone repair of double-strand breaks. In this study aneuploidy inferred from expression is used operationally: a cell is treated as transformed if it is aneuploid. That is how the authors can find transformed cells inside glands that look pre-malignant, and it is why roughly 10 percent of epithelial cells in mutant glands, compared with under 1 percent in wild-type glands, count as already abnormal.

During fetal mammary development there is a basal cell that already expresses the basal keratins KRT5 and KRT14 and TP63 but has not yet acquired the contractile machinery (ACTA2, TAGLN, MYLK) of a mature myoepithelial cell. The tumor basal cells in this paper look like that fetal cell. Two explanations are possible: a leftover fetal population expands, or mature basal-myoepithelial cells go backwards and lose their myoepithelial identity, which is what de-differentiation means. The authors favor de-differentiation because pre-tumor aneuploid cells are mostly mature Bmyo and LumSec cells with few basal or hybrid cells, so the fetal-like population appears to be generated rather than selected.

Pseudo-bulk means taking single-cell data and adding the counts back up across all the cells of a sample, or of one chosen cell population, to produce a single expression profile like the one a bulk RNA sequencing experiment would have given. It is done when you need to use a tool or a reference that was built for bulk data, as here with the human TNBC subtype classifier. The trade-off is that it throws away the cell-level resolution, and it becomes sensitive to sample composition: a tumor with more stroma will produce a different pseudo-bulk profile even if its tumor cells are identical, which the authors note as a reason bulk subtype calls can be unstable.

Instead of waiting for a primary tumor to spread on its own, tumor cells are injected directly into the left ventricle of the heart, so that they are distributed by the arterial circulation to many organs at once. This produces lesions in lung, liver, brain and elsewhere within weeks and is efficient for studying what cells do once they arrive. It deliberately skips the early steps of metastasis, namely escaping the primary tumor, invading, and entering the bloodstream. The authors therefore present their metastasis result as a statement about differentiation state at the secondary site, not as a measurement of metastatic competence.

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.title: Single-cell atlas of the Wap-Cre Brca1/p53 mammary gland and tumors, compared with the Blg-Cre model
figures.question: What cell types are present in Wap-Cre Brca1/p53 glands and tumors, and do the tumor cells of the Wap-Cre and Blg-Cre models occupy the same position on the basal to luminal differentiation axis?
figures.how_to_read: Panel a is the allele design, showing loxP sites around Brca1 exon 10 and p53 exons 5 and 6. Panel b is the mammary phenotype and spontaneous tumor development, panel c the tumor collection across 1 to 25 mm, and panel d the publicly available Blg-Cre dataset spanning wild-type, mutant and tumor samples. Panel e is a UMAP, a two-dimensional map in which cells with similar overall gene expression are placed near each other, colored by the 12 annotated cell types. Panels f and g give cell-type frequencies across wild-type, mutant and tumor conditions. Panels h to j cover the Wap-Cre epithelium re-clustered down to basal-myoepithelial, secretory luminal and tumor cells, with panel i scoring those cells on a composite axis that runs from basal-myoepithelial at one end to secretory luminal at the other, and panel j showing marker expression. Panels k to m are the identical analysis for Blg-Cre, so the two models can be read side by side.
figures.key_result: After quality control 62,195 cells resolved into 12 cell types: four stromal (Schwann cells by Plp1, endothelium by Pecam1, pericytes by Rgs5, fibroblasts by Lum), four immune (B cells by Igkc, T cells by Cd3e, neutrophils by Cxcl2, myeloid cells by Ctss), three normal epithelial (Bmyo by Krt14 and Acta2, LumSec by Wfdc18 and Kit, LumHS by Esr1 and Pgr) and one additional intermediate population that bridges Bmyo and LumSec. That intermediate population is aneuploid by CopyKAT and makes up about 10 percent of epithelial cells in mutant tissue against under 1 percent in wild-type glands. Tumor cells lack Esr1, Pgr and Erbb2, confirming triple-negative status, and express both LumSec (Wfdc18) and a broad basal set (Krt14, Krt5, Krt42, Trp63, Lgals7, Nkain3) wider than what had been reported for Blg-Cre. Reprocessing the Blg-Cre data through the same pipeline also gave 12 cell types but with a discrete aneuploid tumor cluster that does not bridge Bmyo and LumSec. On the composite differentiation axis Wap-Cre tumor cells score toward the Bmyo end and Blg-Cre tumor cells toward the LumSec end, with Blg-Cre tumors carrying lower Krt5 and Trp63 and higher Wfdc18, Krt8 and Ehf. Tumors were also enriched for myeloid cells, T cells and neutrophils, neutrophils expanding only in tumors, with T cells declining as tumors grew.

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.title: Wap-Cre tumors correspond to the mesenchymal TNBC subtype and Blg-Cre tumors to basal-like 1, and BRCA1 carriers develop all subtypes
figures.question: Do the two mouse models map onto different human TNBC subtypes, and do human BRCA1 carriers in fact develop more than one subtype?
figures.how_to_read: Panel a frames the comparison between the two mouse models and human BRCA1 carrier TNBC, and panel b lists the biological programs tied to each TNBC subtype. Panel c gives subtype proportions in BRCA1 carriers against sporadic TNBC in the BGFR and TCGA cohorts. Panel d is the subtype assignment of pseudo-bulked mouse tumors, so one point is one animal. Panels e and f give the single-cell subtype composition of the tumor epithelium in each model, which shows how mixed an individual tumor is. Panel g scores a human mesenchymal signature across BGFR subtypes as a sanity check on that signature. Panels h and i score mouse-derived signatures, one from each model, across the human tumors in both cohorts. Panel j compares expression of mesenchymal, basal-myoepithelial and secretory luminal genes across the models and the human tumors.
figures.key_result: In the human cohorts, 51 BGFR TNBC patients (35 BRCA1 carriers and 16 non-carriers, of whom 34 are newly reported) and 132 TCGA TNBC patients (12 carriers) show that BRCA1 carriers develop all four TNBC subtypes in roughly the same proportions as sporadic TNBC, so carrier disease is not a single entity. Pseudo-bulk subtyping assigned 5 of 7 Wap-Cre tumors to the mesenchymal subtype and the Blg-Cre tumors to basal-like 1. Single-cell subtyping showed intra-tumor heterogeneity in both models, with the dominant epithelial subtype sometimes differing from the tissue-level call, but a consistently higher frequency of mesenchymal-like cells in Wap-Cre tumors. The Wap-Cre epithelial signature scored highest in human mesenchymal TNBC in both cohorts (BGFR P = 0.0081, TCGA P = 0.0068) while the Blg-Cre signature did not. At the gene level Wap-Cre tumors carried higher Setbp1, Etv5 and Kirrel3 than Blg-Cre tumors, and both Wap-Cre and human mesenchymal tumors showed higher basal and lower secretory luminal gene expression. The authors note the circularity that because the classifier selected which tumors contributed to the mouse signature, this analysis supports rather than independently tests the subtype assignments.

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.title: Aberrant basal differentiation is already present in pre-malignant Wap-Cre glands, and the Wap-Cre driver recombines both basal and luminal cells
figures.question: Does the abnormal basal state appear before tumors form, and could it instead be an artifact of where the Wap-Cre driver is active?
figures.how_to_read: Panels a to h identify aneuploid cells in pre-malignant glands of both models and place them on the cell-type map. Panels i and j characterize the Wap-Cre aneuploid cells by marker and signature expression and by position on the basal to luminal axis; panels k and l do the same for Blg-Cre. Panels m and n give the TNBC subtype assignment of these pre-malignant aneuploid cells, split by the normal cell type they most resemble. Panels o and p report the single-cell genotyping result, that is, which cell types carry the recombined allele.
figures.key_result: Aneuploid cells are present in mutant glands of both models before any overt tumor. In Wap-Cre they are heterogeneous, most falling in a tumor-like cluster closer to Bmyo cells, expressing basal and mesenchymal-subtype genes and scoring toward the Bmyo end of the differentiation axis. In Blg-Cre most aneuploid cells cluster with secretory luminal cells, express luminal markers and do not express mesenchymal-subtype genes. Subtype assignment of these early cells already splits the models: Wap-Cre tumor-like cells are mostly mesenchymal and Blg-Cre tumor-like cells mostly basal-like 1, and within mutant glands of both models the secretory luminal cells are enriched for basal-like 1 assignment while the basal-myoepithelial cells are enriched for mesenchymal assignment. The genotyping is the critical control: because Brca1 is too large for multiplexed PCR, the authors adapted MAESTER to read the Trp53 transcript, which the same Wap-Cre driver recombines, and found recombined alleles in both Bmyo and LumSec cells of Wap-Cre mutants. Restricted Cre recombination therefore does not explain the basal phenotype. The same genotyping could not be applied to the published Blg-Cre dataset because it needs physical material, so the claim that only luminal cells transform in that model rests on copy-number inference.

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.title: Only transplanted basal cells give rise to tumors containing basal cells, matching spontaneous Wap-Cre tumors
figures.question: Which sorted epithelial fraction from a pre-tumor mutant gland actually generates a tumor with the composition of a spontaneous Wap-Cre tumor?
figures.how_to_read: Panel a is the transplantation design, basal and luminal cells from pre-tumor Wap-Cre donors into cleared fat pads of NSG recipients. Panel b is the flow cytometry gating that defines the two fractions. Panels c to e are single-cell RNA sequencing of the sorted fractions, confirming that the separation worked and quantifying aneuploid content in each. Panel f gives tumor formation rates per injection site. Panel g is immunofluorescence of the resulting tumors stained for the basal markers KRT14 and TP63, the luminal marker KRT8, and cells carrying both.
figures.key_result: Sorting was clean with minimal cross-contamination, and both fractions contained comparable numbers of aneuploid cells, so neither fraction was handicapped at the start. Basal cells produced tumors at 7 of 10 injection sites and luminal cells at 3 of 8, a difference that is not statistically significant (two-sided Fisher exact P = 0.34), and tumors from the two fractions reached comparable mass. The composition is what separates them: all 7 basal-derived tumors contained KRT14 positive TP63 positive basal cells, and none of the 3 luminal-derived tumors did, while both fractions produced KRT8 positive luminal cells and hybrid cells expressing both. Spontaneous Wap-Cre tumors in intact mice show the same pattern as the basal-derived tumors. The authors connect this to the observation that 2 of 7 spontaneous tumors were not mesenchymal subtype, consistent with a minority of spontaneous tumors arising from luminal cells. Because donors were matched and alleles identical across the two fractions, this is the comparison in the paper that isolates cell of origin from Cre driver and allele differences.

figures.label: Fig. 5
figures.title: Transforming basal-myoepithelial cells lose myoepithelial markers and enter a fetal-like basal state
figures.question: Which normal developmental state do the abnormal basal cells resemble, and are they an expanded leftover fetal population or mature cells that went backwards?
figures.how_to_read: Panel a lays out the mouse developmental atlas used as reference, covering fetal, pubertal, adult, gestation, lactation and involution stages plus fetal skin, pubertal ducts and terminal end buds. Panels b and f define the eight epithelial states found in that atlas and show marker expression across them, including the mouse tumor cells. Panel c scores the mesenchymal subtype signature across the developmental states. Panels d and e co-embed the mouse tumor and pre-tumor aneuploid cells with the atlas, so each abnormal cell is assigned to the developmental state it most resembles.
figures.key_result: The atlas resolves eight epithelial states, including a fetal basal state that is Krt5, Krt14 and Trp63 positive but Acta2, Tagln and Mylk negative, a hybrid state co-expressing basal and luminal markers, and lactocytes expressing Csn2 and Wfdc18. The mesenchymal signature scores negative across most states, with Bmyo cells and lactocytes least negative. Blg-Cre aneuploid cells map mainly to secretory luminal cells. Wap-Cre aneuploid tumor cells span many states with a large expansion of fetal basal cells plus hybrid and proliferative cells. Crucially, pre-tumor Wap-Cre aneuploid cells are mostly mature Bmyo and LumSec with few hybrid or basal cells, which the authors read as de-differentiation of Bmyo cells rather than expansion of a residual fetal population. The progression tracks tumor size: the two 1 mm tumors resemble mutant glands and are mostly Bmyo, the 2 mm and 8 mm tumors have more basal and proliferating Bmyo cells, and the three 25 mm tumors have large hybrid, proliferating luminal and secretory luminal populations. Tumor Bmyo cells do not express Acta2, Tagln or Mylk, and that marker loss extends to the hybrid state in both models. Subtyping 5,587 E18 fetal cells showed the fetal epithelium enriched for mesenchymal-like cells across states, with basal-like 1 assignment restricted to the luminal lineage, basal-like 1 associated with proliferation and luminal androgen receptor with hormone-sensing cells.

figures.label: Fig. 6
figures.title: Smooth muscle actin negative basal cells and proliferation concentrate in hyperbranched regions of mutant glands
figures.question: Where in the intact tissue does the abnormal basal state sit, and is it spread uniformly or restricted to particular regions?
figures.how_to_read: Panels a and b introduce the CODEX multiplexed imaging of wild-type glands, mutant glands and small and large tumors. Panel d compares wild-type tissue against the normal-looking and hyperplastic regions of mutant glands. Panels e to g quantify cell states in tumors. Cells are classified from the imaging markers: basal as KRT14 positive, smooth muscle actin positive, KRT8 negative; luminal as KRT14 negative, smooth muscle actin negative, KRT8 positive; proliferation from MKI67. The abnormal fetal-like basal cell appears as KRT14 positive but smooth muscle actin negative.
figures.key_result: Wild-type glands show the expected bilayer of inner luminal and outer basal-myoepithelial cells with no hybrid and no KRT14 positive smooth muscle actin negative cells detected at all. Mutant glands contain two kinds of region: normal-looking regions that do not differ significantly from wild-type, and hyperplastic regions with extensive hyper-branching in which the basal layer lacks smooth muscle actin, matching the fetal-like basal state seen by sequencing. Tumors are highly enriched for smooth muscle actin negative basal cells. Proliferation is infrequent in wild-type tissue and mostly confined to the luminal layer, whereas mutant glands show a high frequency of proliferating cells concentrated in the hyperplastic regions, with the smooth muscle actin negative basal cells proliferating most. The authors state the panel's limitation directly: it cannot distinguish a developmental fetal basal cell from a Bmyo cell that has lost its myoepithelial markers.

figures.label: Fig. 7
figures.title: Metastatic lesions shift toward luminal differentiation while keeping a mesenchymal-like transcriptional program
figures.question: When Wap-Cre tumor cells colonize distant organs, do they keep their differentiation state and their subtype?
figures.how_to_read: Panels a and b describe the design: cells from one late-stage tumor injected into the left ventricle of the heart for multi-organ spread, with orthotopic implants as controls. Panel c shows how donor cells were identified and which samples passed the burden threshold for sequencing. Panels d and e give the cell-state composition of metastatic lesions against the primary tumor. Panel f shows where basal cells were found. Panel g compares marker expression between metastases and the primary tumor.
figures.key_result: Cells from a single late-stage tumor were injected intracardially into 6 NSG mice and orthotopically into 2 controls, with lung, liver, brain and mammary glands harvested at 4 weeks. Donor cells were identified by flow cytometry as H-2Kb positive and H-2Kd negative, and only samples above 0.5 percent metastatic burden were sequenced, yielding 4,806 cells including a donor-tumor control put through the same workflow. Enriched and unenriched profiles were indistinguishable. Metastases were enriched for secretory luminal and proliferating luminal states relative to the primary tumor, with low-burden tissues containing more hybrid cells and high-burden tissues more secretory luminal cells. Basal cells were rarely detected and only in low-burden lung metastases. Marker expression matched the primary tumor, and the mesenchymal subtype distribution in metastases was indistinguishable from the primary and orthotopic tumors. The authors emphasize that with one donor tumor, immunodeficient hosts and an injection route that bypasses the early steps of metastasis, this reports differentiation state at the secondary site rather than metastatic competence.

figures.label: Fig. 8
figures.title: Cross-species integration nominates human basal-myoepithelial and LumSec-myo cells as counterparts of the Wap-Cre cell of origin
figures.question: Which human breast epithelial cell state corresponds to the mouse cell of origin identified here?
figures.how_to_read: Panel b reprocesses the Human Breast Cell Atlas into eight states, one major basal-myoepithelial population and seven secretory luminal subpopulations. Panel c scores the human mesenchymal signature across those states. Panels a, d and e co-embed mouse and human cells so that mouse pre-tumor aneuploid cells and tumor cells can be assigned to the human state they co-cluster with. Panel f checks whether the mouse cells that land with human basal-myoepithelial and LumSec-myo cells actually express the marker that defines those states.
figures.key_result: All eight human states remained identifiable after integration, with LumSec-myo bridging basal and luminal cells, and wild-type mouse cells showing less state diversity with LumSec-major dominant. Human basal-myoepithelial cells scored highest for the human mesenchymal signature, with LumSec-KIT, LumSec-lac, LumSec-myo and LumSec-prol slightly higher than the remaining luminal states. Wap-Cre pre-tumor aneuploid cells clustered mostly with human basal-myoepithelial cells while Blg-Cre cells clustered mostly with LumSec-major, and the tumors followed the same split, with Wap-Cre tumors basal-like across Bmyo, LumSec-basal and LumSec-myo and Blg-Cre tumors mostly LumSec-major. Wap-Cre metastases resembled LumSec-major, LumSec-myo and LumSec-prol. Pseudo-bulk subtyping of the human states themselves assigned basal-myoepithelial as mesenchymal-like, secretory luminal as basal-like 1, and LumSec-myo as mesenchymal-like, which is why the authors propose that mesenchymal tumors originate in either basal-myoepithelial or LumSec-myo cells. The marker check in panel f is a caution rather than a confirmation: the mouse cells co-clustering with human Bmyo and LumSec-myo do not express Acta2, the gene that defines those states, so the correspondence is partial.

key_findings.statement: Tumors in the Wap-Cre Brca1/p53 model carry a broad basal program and sit on a continuum between basal-myoepithelial and secretory luminal identity, whereas tumors in the Blg-Cre model form a discrete secretory luminal cluster, even when both datasets are processed through an identical pipeline.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 1e to 1m. 62,195 cells after quality control, 12 cell types, an aneuploid intermediate population bridging Bmyo and LumSec that is about 10 percent of mutant epithelium versus under 1 percent of wild-type, tumor expression of Krt14, Krt5, Krt42, Trp63, Lgals7 and Nkain3 alongside Wfdc18, and opposite positions of the two models on the composite basal to luminal axis.

key_findings.statement: Wap-Cre tumors correspond to the mesenchymal subtype of human TNBC and Blg-Cre tumors to basal-like 1, so the two mouse models model different human diseases rather than the same one.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 2d gives 5 of 7 Wap-Cre tumors as mesenchymal and the Blg-Cre tumors as basal-like 1. Fig. 2h and 2i show the Wap-Cre epithelial signature scoring highest in human mesenchymal TNBC in both cohorts (BGFR P = 0.0081, TCGA P = 0.0068) while the Blg-Cre signature does not. Fig. 2e and 2f show the same split at single-cell resolution.

key_findings.statement: Human BRCA1 carriers develop all four TNBC subtypes at roughly the same proportions as patients with sporadic TNBC, so no single subtype can be taken as the carrier phenotype.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 2c, using 51 BGFR TNBC patients (35 BRCA1 carriers, 16 non-carriers, 34 newly reported) and 132 TCGA TNBC patients (12 carriers), with subtypes assigned by highest centroid correlation.

key_findings.statement: The basal phenotype of Wap-Cre tumors is not an artifact of restricted Cre activity, because both basal-myoepithelial and secretory luminal cells in mutant Wap-Cre glands carry the recombined allele.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 3o and 3p, single-cell genotyping using MAESTER adapted to read the Trp53 transcript, which the same Wap-Cre driver recombines, since Brca1 is too large for multiplexed PCR.

key_findings.statement: Only the sorted basal fraction from pre-tumor mutant glands produces tumors that contain basal cells, matching the composition of spontaneous Wap-Cre tumors, even though basal and luminal fractions form tumors at statistically indistinguishable rates.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 4f and 4g. Basal gave tumors at 7 of 10 injection sites and luminal at 3 of 8 (two-sided Fisher exact P = 0.34); all 7 basal-derived tumors contained KRT14 positive TP63 positive cells and none of the 3 luminal-derived tumors did. Donors were matched and alleles identical across fractions, across two independent experiments.

key_findings.statement: Aberrant basal differentiation precedes tumor formation: aneuploid cells are already present in mutant glands with no visible tumor, and in Wap-Cre they are basal-leaning and already mesenchymal-subtype-like.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 3a to 3n, with CopyKAT-inferred aneuploidy in pre-malignant glands of both models, Wap-Cre aneuploid cells scoring toward the Bmyo end of the axis and assigned mostly mesenchymal, Blg-Cre aneuploid cells clustering with LumSec and assigned mostly basal-like 1.

key_findings.statement: Basal-myoepithelial cells de-differentiate during transformation, losing the myoepithelial markers Acta2, Tagln and Mylk and entering a state that resembles fetal basal cells rather than any adult or gestational state.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 5b to 5f against the mouse developmental atlas (GEO GSE164017), with the fetal basal state defined as Krt5, Krt14 and Trp63 positive but Acta2, Tagln and Mylk negative, expansion of that state in Wap-Cre tumor cells, and loss of the three myoepithelial markers in tumor Bmyo and hybrid cells in both models. Pre-tumor aneuploid cells are mostly mature Bmyo and LumSec with few basal or hybrid cells, which argues for de-differentiation rather than expansion of a residual fetal population.

key_findings.statement: The abnormal smooth muscle actin negative basal cells and most of the proliferation are spatially confined to hyperbranched hyperplastic regions of mutant glands, while other regions of the same gland look normal.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 6d to 6g by CODEX multiplexed imaging. Wild-type glands contain no KRT14 positive smooth muscle actin negative cells at all, mutant glands separate into normal-looking regions indistinguishable from wild-type and hyperplastic regions whose basal layer lacks smooth muscle actin, and tumors are highly enriched for those cells. Extended Data Fig. 6a and 6c cover proliferation.

key_findings.statement: Metastatic lesions shift toward luminal differentiation states but keep the mesenchymal-like transcriptional program and subtype of the primary tumor.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 7d to 7g and Extended Data Fig. 7e and 7f. 4,806 cells from intracardiac metastases in 6 NSG mice plus 2 orthotopic controls from one donor tumor, with enrichment for secretory luminal and proliferating luminal states, basal cells only in low-burden lung lesions, and a mesenchymal subtype distribution indistinguishable from primary and orthotopic tumors.

key_findings.statement: Human basal-myoepithelial cells and the LumSec-myo state are the leading candidate human counterparts of the Wap-Cre cell of origin, but neither can be confirmed.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 8c to 8f against the Human Breast Cell Atlas (GEO GSE235326). Human Bmyo cells score highest for the mesenchymal signature, Wap-Cre pre-tumor aneuploid cells co-cluster with human Bmyo, and pseudo-bulk subtyping calls Bmyo and LumSec-myo mesenchymal-like while LumSec is basal-like 1. The caution is in Fig. 8f: the mouse cells landing with human Bmyo and LumSec-myo do not express Acta2, the gene defining those states.

limitations: The comparison between the Wap-Cre and Blg-Cre models confounds cell of origin with two other differences, a different Cre driver and different floxed Brca1 and p53 alleles, so it cannot by itself attribute the subtype difference to cell of origin. The authors are explicit that only the within-Wap-Cre transplantation, with matched donors and identical alleles, isolates that variable.

Single-cell genotyping needs physical tissue and could not be applied to the published Blg-Cre dataset, so the claim that only secretory luminal cells transform in that model rests on copy-number inference from expression rather than on direct genotype.

The CODEX antibody panel cannot distinguish a genuinely developmental fetal basal cell from a basal-myoepithelial cell that has simply lost its myoepithelial markers, which is exactly the distinction the de-differentiation argument turns on.

The metastasis experiment uses cells from a single donor tumor in immunodeficient NSG recipients, and intracardiac injection bypasses escape from the primary tumor, invasion and intravasation, so it reports differentiation state at the secondary site rather than metastatic competence. It also included no therapy, so it cannot address treatment-driven subtype switching.

Transplantation incidence did not differ significantly between the basal and luminal fractions (7 of 10 versus 3 of 8, Fisher exact P = 0.34), so the argument rests on tumor composition rather than on tumor-forming efficiency, with small numbers of recipients.

Because the subtype classifier selected which tumors contributed to the mouse mesenchymal signature, the signature scoring in the human cohorts supports the subtype assignments rather than testing them independently.

Bulk and pseudo-bulk subtype classification is sensitive to how much stroma is in a sample while single-cell subtyping is not, and baseline subtype distributions differ between models and between species, so subtype calls must be read against the baseline of their own dataset.

The mutational landscape of the Wap-Cre tumors was not profiled, so the claim that mutation does not specify subtype is an inference from the convergence of these tumors on one subtype rather than a direct test.

The human counterpart of the mouse cell of origin remains unresolved between basal-myoepithelial and LumSec-myo cells, because mouse and human epithelial states correspond only weakly, and the authors state that settling it would require human lineage tracing, which is not currently feasible.
open_questions: Is the fetal-like basal state permissive for transformation, meaning it comes first and allows malignancy, or is it a consequence of transformation? The authors say lineage tracing is needed to separate these and that their data cannot.

Which human cell state is the true counterpart of the Wap-Cre cell of origin, basal-myoepithelial or LumSec-myo, given that the mouse cells mapping to both fail to express Acta2, the marker that defines them?

Would a direct lineage-tracing experiment in the Wap-Cre model, marking basal-myoepithelial cells heritably rather than relying on transplantation, confirm a basal origin in an intact immunocompetent animal?
Does BRCA1 loss drive the loss of myoepithelial identity through its effect on hormone receptor degradation, which is the mechanism the introduction proposes but the paper never tests?

If subtype is set at initiation, why do mesenchymal TNBCs frequently switch subtype at recurrence or metastasis in patients, and is that a real change in tumor cells or an artifact of stromal content in bulk classification?
Does a basal-myoepithelial origin have treatment consequences, for instance a different response to PARP inhibitors or checkpoint blockade than a luminal-origin basal-like 1 tumor?
reading.relevance_to_lab: This is the lab's own central question, addressed head on in the model system the lab works in, and it argues against the position the field has held since the luminal progenitor work of the late 2000s and 2010s. The standard claim, built on human carrier tissue profiling and on the Blg-Cre Brca1/p53 mouse, is that BRCA1-associated TNBC arises from luminal progenitors. This paper does not overturn that so much as narrow it: it accepts that Blg-Cre luminal-origin tumors are real and shows that they correspond specifically to the basal-like 1 subtype, while adding the basal-myoepithelial compartment as a second origin that produces mesenchymal TNBC. Since BRCA1 carriers in the BGFR and TCGA cohorts develop all four subtypes at roughly sporadic proportions, the implication for the lab is that a single cell of origin was never going to account for carrier disease, and that any statement about the cell of origin should be paired with a subtype. Three things are directly usable. First, the methodological warning about Cre drivers: Wap is treated as a secretory luminal promoter, which is why the authors expected a luminal origin, yet single-cell genotyping of the recombined Trp53 allele found recombination in basal-myoepithelial cells as well. Any cell-of-origin claim the lab makes from a Cre driver, including its own, should be checked this way rather than assumed, and the MAESTER adaptation that reads Trp53 instead of Brca1, because Brca1 is too large for multiplexed PCR, is a protocol the lab could copy straight across to its own models. Second, the warning about reading origin off markers: tumor basal cells here lose Acta2, Tagln and Mylk, so a Bmyo-derived tumor does not look like a mature Bmyo cell, and in the human atlas integration the mouse cells landing with human Bmyo and LumSec-myo fail to express Acta2. A lab scoring its own scRNA-seq for a luminal progenitor origin using mature-lineage markers would miss basal-derived disease entirely. Third, the strength-of-evidence ranking is worth adopting: the authors themselves say the Wap-Cre versus Blg-Cre comparison confounds cell of origin with Cre driver and allele, and that only the within-model transplantation of matched sorted fractions isolates it, and the lab should hold the paper and itself to that standard. The reanalysis of the published Blg-Cre data is where the lab should look hardest, because what it actually shows is more limited than the headline: run through an identical pipeline, Blg-Cre aneuploid cells cluster with secretory luminal cells and the tumor cluster is discrete rather than bridging, and Blg-Cre tumors carry lower Krt5 and Trp63 and higher Wfdc18, Krt8 and Ehf. But the claim that only luminal cells transform in that model comes from CopyKAT copy-number inference alone, because genotyping needs physical tissue the authors did not have. So the Blg-Cre arm of the comparison is inference, not genotype, and the lab is well placed to test it directly if it can genotype its own Blg-Cre or equivalent material. On the evidence that aberrant differentiation precedes tumor formation, the case is reasonable but not closed: aneuploid cells are present in 4-month-old mutant glands with no visible tumor and already lean basal and mesenchymal-like, the pre-tumor aneuploid population is mostly mature Bmyo and LumSec with few hybrid or fetal-like basal cells, which argues that the fetal-like state is generated rather than selected from a leftover population, and CODEX localizes smooth muscle actin negative basal cells and most proliferation to hyperbranched hyperplastic regions of mutant glands while neighboring regions look normal. The authors concede they cannot say whether the fetal-like state permits transformation or follows it, and that their imaging panel cannot tell a developmental fetal basal cell from a Bmyo cell that lost its markers. On the lab's second thread, immune evasion, this paper tests nothing. There is no analysis of cGAS-STING, NF-kB or IRF3, no type I interferon scoring, no MHC class I, B2m, Nlrc5, HLA-C, HLA-E or NKG2A, and no natural killer or CD8 T cell work. Immune cells appear only as cluster abundances: myeloid cells, T cells and neutrophils are enriched in tumors, neutrophils expand only in tumors, myeloid and T cells are already increased in some mutant glands, and T cells decline as tumors grow, all tested with Milo differential abundance. H-2Kb and H-2Kd appear only as strain markers for telling donor from host cells in the metastasis assay, not as antigen presentation readouts. Worth noting for interpretation: the transplantation and metastasis experiments both used NSG recipients, which lack adaptive immunity and functional natural killer cells, so the only immunocompetent material in the paper is the spontaneous Wap-Cre glands and tumors, and that is the only part of the dataset where an immune surveillance question could be asked. If the lab wants to overlay its interferon and MHC class I panel, the specific cell states to score are: basal-myoepithelial cells in wild-type versus mutant glands; the fetal-like basal state defined as Krt5, Krt14 and Trp63 positive but Acta2, Tagln and Mylk negative, which is the state the lab's model would predict is where cytosolic DNA first accumulates; the aneuploid intermediate population that bridges Bmyo and LumSec and makes up about 10 percent of mutant epithelium against under 1 percent of wild-type, which is the earliest transformed population available; the hybrid state; secretory luminal cells and the proliferating luminal state; and in the human frame the Human Breast Cell Atlas states Bmyo, LumSec-myo, LumSec-basal and LumSec-KIT. The spatial comparison of hyperplastic against normal-looking regions within the same mutant gland is a natural internal control for any interferon score, since the two regions differ in the abnormal basal state but share the animal. On data access, this is the main practical limitation: the retrievable text contains no data availability statement and no accession for this study's own single-cell data, so the lab cannot yet assume it can reanalyse the 67,001 cells and should check the deposited version or write to Devon Lawson at UC Irvine. What is immediately reusable are the external resources the paper leans on, all public: the mouse mammary developmental atlas at GEO GSE164017, which is what defines the fetal basal state and is the reference the lab would need to reproduce the de-differentiation argument, the Human Breast Cell Atlas at GEO GSE235326, TCGA-BRCA through UCSC Xena, and the Vanderbilt TNBCtype classifier. The BGFR cohort of 51 TNBC patients curated by the Nathanson laboratory at Penn has no public accession in what was retrievable. Two smaller borrowings: the composite basal to luminal axis score, built from the top 500 marker genes of each wild-type population and rescaled so one axis runs from Bmyo to LumSec, is a cleaner way to place tumor cells than cluster labels, and the gene-level differences the paper reports between models, higher Setbp1, Etv5 and Kirrel3 in Wap-Cre tumors, are concrete things to check in the lab's own data. One citation caveat: the retrievable introduction cites only numbered references, and the canonical luminal progenitor papers that the lab would expect to see argued against are not named in the text, so the reference list should be checked before assuming how the authors position themselves against that literature.
discussion_questions: The authors concede that Wap-Cre versus Blg-Cre confounds cell of origin with Cre driver and with different floxed Brca1 and p53 alleles, and that only the within-model transplantation isolates origin. That transplantation gave 7 of 10 basal sites versus 3 of 8 luminal sites, which is not significant (P = 0.34), so the claim rests entirely on tumor composition: all 7 basal-derived tumors contained KRT14 positive TP63 positive cells and none of the 3 luminal-derived tumors did. Is composition from 10 implants enough to establish a second cell of origin, and what would we want to see added, more recipients, limiting dilution, or heritable lineage tracing in an intact animal?

The claim that only secretory luminal cells transform in the Blg-Cre model comes from CopyKAT copy-number inference, because the authors could not genotype a published dataset. We can genotype our own material. Should we run the MAESTER-style single-cell genotyping on our own Cre models, reading Trp53 as the proxy since Brca1 is too large for multiplexed PCR, to find out whether our drivers are as compartment-specific as we have been assuming?

Tumor basal cells here lose Acta2, Tagln and Mylk, and the mouse cells that map onto human Bmyo and LumSec-myo also fail to express Acta2. If a basal-myoepithelial-derived tumor no longer looks like a mature myoepithelial cell, how much of our own evidence for a luminal progenitor origin depends on mature-lineage markers that a de-differentiated basal cell would also fail, and can we re-score our datasets on the paper's basal to luminal axis instead of on cluster labels?

This paper tests no immune step at all: no cGAS-STING, no interferon, no MHC class I, no NK or CD8 work, and both the transplantation and metastasis experiments used NSG recipients with no adaptive or NK immunity. If our model is BRCA1 loss leading to cytosolic DNA, then cGAS-STING, then NF-kB and IRF3, then type I interferon, then MHC class I suppression, then loss of NK and CD8 surveillance, does the fetal-like basal state, Krt14 and Trp63 positive but Acta2, Tagln and Mylk negative, make a sharper prediction than the luminal progenitor does about where that cascade starts, and is the hyperplastic versus normal-looking region comparison within one mutant gland the right internal control for testing it?

If subtype is specified at initiation, as the persistence of the mesenchymal program across tumor size, transplantation and metastasis suggests, that sits awkwardly with the clinical observation that mesenchymal TNBCs frequently switch subtype at recurrence. The authors offer stromal content in bulk classification as one explanation, and their own metastasis experiment used one donor tumor with no therapy. How would we design a test that separates genuine plasticity from a classification artifact, and does it change whether we should be subtyping our own tumors by pseudo-bulk or by single cell?

The paper's prevention argument is that strategies aimed only at luminal progenitors would leave the basal compartment untouched. Does this change what we think a prophylactic intervention in BRCA1 carriers would have to reach, and is there a readout in carrier tissue, such as smooth muscle actin negative basal cells in hyperbranched regions, that could be looked for in risk-reducing mastectomy specimens we have access to?

nodes.label: What decides TNBC subtype in BRCA1 carriers?
nodes.detail: Triple-negative breast cancer splits into four transcriptional subtypes with different prognosis and drug response, but what determines which subtype a tumor becomes was unknown, and subtype is not used to stratify BRCA1 carriers.

nodes.label: Field holds that luminal progenitors are the origin
nodes.detail: The Blg-Cre Brca1/p53 mouse, in which Brca1 is deleted in luminal progenitors and gives invasive ductal-like tumors, has dominated the field, while Krt14-Cre deletion in basal cells gives metaplastic-like tumors that are rare in human carriers.

nodes.label: BRCA1 degrades hormone receptors, so differentiation may matter
nodes.detail: Genomic instability alone does not explain why BRCA1 risk concentrates in hormone-responsive organs. BRCA1 has an E3 ubiquitin ligase domain that targets hormone receptors for degradation, and hormone receptors direct epithelial differentiation, which points to a non-genetic route to initiation.

nodes.label: Cell of origin sets subtype through aberrant differentiation
nodes.detail: The authors propose that the epithelial compartment in which BRCA1 is lost determines the subtype of the resulting TNBC, by setting the aberrant differentiation trajectory the transforming cells follow.

nodes.label: scRNA-seq of Wap-Cre model plus identical reanalysis of Blg-Cre
nodes.detail: The under-characterized Wap-Cre Brca1 f10/f10 p53 f5and6/f5and6 model was profiled by multiplexed single-cell RNA sequencing across wild-type glands, pre-tumor mutant glands and tumors from 1 to 25 mm, and the published Blg-Cre data were reprocessed through the same pipeline. Because Wap is a secretory luminal promoter, a luminal origin was expected.

nodes.label: Wap-Cre tumors are basal-leaning, Blg-Cre tumors are discretely luminal
nodes.detail: Of 62,195 cells, 12 cell types were resolved including an aneuploid population bridging basal-myoepithelial and secretory luminal identity that is about 10 percent of mutant epithelium against under 1 percent of wild-type. Wap-Cre tumor cells score toward the basal-myoepithelial end of a composite differentiation axis while Blg-Cre tumor cells score toward the secretory luminal end.

nodes.label: Wap-Cre maps to TNBC-M, Blg-Cre to TNBC-BL1
nodes.detail: Pseudo-bulk subtyping assigned 5 of 7 Wap-Cre tumors to the mesenchymal subtype and the Blg-Cre tumors to basal-like 1, and the Wap-Cre epithelial signature scored highest in human mesenchymal TNBC in both clinical cohorts while the Blg-Cre signature did not.

nodes.label: Carriers develop all four subtypes at sporadic proportions
nodes.detail: Across 51 BGFR TNBC patients and 132 TCGA TNBC patients, BRCA1 carriers developed all four TNBC subtypes at roughly the same proportions as patients with sporadic TNBC, so both mouse models correspond to real carrier disease.

nodes.label: Aberrant basal differentiation precedes any visible tumor
nodes.detail: Aneuploid cells are already present in 4-month-old mutant glands with no overt tumor. In Wap-Cre they lean basal and already score as mesenchymal-like, while in Blg-Cre they cluster with secretory luminal cells and score as basal-like 1.

nodes.label: Wap-Cre recombines basal cells too, so Cre pattern is not the explanation
nodes.detail: Single-cell genotyping, using MAESTER adapted to read the Trp53 transcript because Brca1 is too large for multiplexed PCR, found recombined alleles in both basal-myoepithelial and secretory luminal cells of mutant Wap-Cre glands.

nodes.label: Only transplanted basal cells make tumors containing basal cells
nodes.detail: Basal and luminal fractions sorted from matched pre-tumor mutant donors formed tumors at statistically indistinguishable rates (7 of 10 versus 3 of 8, P = 0.34), but all 7 basal-derived tumors contained KRT14 positive TP63 positive cells and none of the 3 luminal-derived tumors did, matching spontaneous Wap-Cre tumors.

nodes.label: Transforming Bmyo cells lose myoepithelial markers and look fetal
nodes.detail: Tumor basal-myoepithelial cells do not express Acta2, Tagln or Mylk and resemble a fetal basal state in a developmental atlas. Pre-tumor aneuploid cells are mostly mature Bmyo and LumSec with few hybrid or basal cells, which argues for de-differentiation rather than expansion of a residual fetal population. Multiplexed imaging places these smooth muscle actin negative basal cells, and most of the proliferation, in hyperbranched hyperplastic regions of mutant glands, while other regions of the same gland look like wild-type.

nodes.label: Human Bmyo and LumSec-myo are candidate counterparts
nodes.detail: In cross-species integration with the Human Breast Cell Atlas, human basal-myoepithelial cells scored highest for the mesenchymal signature, Wap-Cre pre-tumor aneuploid cells co-clustered with them, and pseudo-bulk subtyping called Bmyo and LumSec-myo mesenchymal-like while secretory luminal was basal-like 1.

nodes.label: Cell of origin shapes TNBC subtype; Bmyo gives TNBC-M
nodes.detail: Basal-myoepithelial cells are a second cell of origin for BRCA1-associated TNBC, giving the mesenchymal subtype, while secretory luminal origin gives basal-like 1. Basal-derived BRCA1 disease is therefore not restricted to metaplastic breast cancer.

nodes.label: Subtype looks specified at initiation, not by later mutation
nodes.detail: The mesenchymal program persists across tumor size, differentiation state, transplantation and metastasis, and Wap-Cre tumors converge on one subtype despite genomic heterogeneity, which the authors read as specification at initiation. In the metastasis assay, lesions shifted toward secretory luminal and proliferating luminal states yet kept a subtype distribution indistinguishable from the primary tumor. The mutational landscape of these tumors was not profiled.

nodes.label: Prevention must cover both compartments; subtype should stratify carriers
nodes.detail: Because disease can start in more than one epithelial compartment, a prevention strategy aimed only at luminal progenitors would leave the basal-myoepithelial compartment untouched. And because carriers develop all four subtypes, which differ in prognosis and drug response, the authors argue subtype should be used to stratify carriers rather than treating carrier disease as one entity.

entities.name: BRCA1
entities.description: Tumor suppressor whose loss drives error-prone DNA repair and copy-number change, and which also targets hormone receptors for degradation; conditionally deleted in the mouse models studied here.

entities.name: TP53
entities.description: Tumor suppressor, the most common co-mutation in BRCA1 breast cancer, deleted alongside Brca1 in both mouse models and used here as the proxy transcript for single-cell genotyping.

entities.name: Wap-Cre Brca1/p53 mouse
entities.description: Conditional mouse model with loxP sites around Brca1 exon 10 and p53 exons 5 and 6, driven by the Wap promoter, which this paper shows gives rise to mesenchymal-subtype TNBC from basal-myoepithelial cells.

entities.name: Blg-Cre Brca1/p53 mouse
entities.description: The field's dominant BRCA1 model, with Brca1 exons 21 to 23 floxed and Cre driven in luminal progenitors, reanalyzed here and shown to give basal-like 1 subtype tumors.

entities.name: Basal-myoepithelial cell (Bmyo)
entities.description: The contractile outer layer of the mammary epithelium, marked by KRT5, KRT14, TP63, ACTA2, TAGLN and MYLK, proposed here as a second cell of origin for BRCA1-associated TNBC.

entities.name: Secretory luminal cell (LumSec, luminal progenitor)
entities.description: Hormone-receptor-negative inner luminal cell marked by KIT and mouse Wfdc18, long held to be the cell of origin of BRCA1 TNBC and shown here to give the basal-like 1 subtype.

entities.name: Luminal hormone-sensing cell (LumHS)
entities.description: Inner luminal cell carrying ESR1 and PGR, present in the atlas but excluded from the copy-number and cross-species analyses in this paper.

entities.name: Fetal-like basal state
entities.description: A KRT5, KRT14 and TP63 positive but ACTA2, TAGLN and MYLK negative state found in fetal mammary development and expanded in Wap-Cre tumors, which the authors argue arises by de-differentiation of basal-myoepithelial cells.

entities.name: Hybrid basal-luminal state
entities.description: A state co-expressing basal and luminal markers, found in the developmental atlas, expanded in large Wap-Cre tumors, and also losing myoepithelial markers in both mouse models.

entities.name: Aneuploid intermediate population
entities.description: A copy-number-abnormal population bridging basal-myoepithelial and secretory luminal identity, making up about 10 percent of epithelial cells in mutant Wap-Cre glands against under 1 percent in wild-type, and the earliest transformed population in the dataset.

entities.name: LumSec-myo
entities.description: A human secretory luminal subpopulation in the Human Breast Cell Atlas that bridges basal and luminal cells and classifies as mesenchymal-like, nominated alongside human Bmyo as a candidate counterpart of the Wap-Cre cell of origin.

entities.name: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)
entities.description: Breast cancer lacking estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2, which presents younger and relapses more often, and is the disease class both mouse models produce.

entities.name: TNBC mesenchymal subtype (TNBC-M)
entities.description: TNBC subtype associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition, stem-like programs and distant metastasis, assigned here to 5 of 7 Wap-Cre tumors and to human basal-myoepithelial and LumSec-myo pseudo-bulk profiles.

entities.name: TNBC basal-like 1 subtype (TNBC-BL1)
entities.description: Proliferation-associated TNBC subtype, assigned here to Blg-Cre tumors and to human secretory luminal pseudo-bulk profiles, and restricted to the luminal lineage in fetal tissue.

entities.name: Ductal hyperplasia with hyperbranching
entities.description: The pre-malignant mammary phenotype of Wap-Cre mutant mice, including excess side branching and precocious alveolar formation, and the spatial location of the abnormal smooth muscle actin negative basal cells.

entities.name: Mammary gland
entities.description: The organ studied, whose bilayered epithelium of outer basal-myoepithelial and inner luminal cells is the setting for the cell-of-origin question.

entities.name: KRT14
entities.description: Basal keratin used throughout as the defining marker of basal identity, in sequencing, in immunofluorescence of transplant-derived tumors and in CODEX imaging.

entities.name: TP63
entities.description: Basal transcription factor, co-stained with KRT14 to score whether a transplant-derived tumor contains basal cells.

entities.name: ACTA2
entities.description: Smooth muscle actin, the myoepithelial contractile marker whose loss, together with TAGLN and MYLK, defines the fetal-like basal state in both the sequencing and the spatial imaging data.

entities.name: KRT5
entities.description: Basal keratin, higher in Wap-Cre tumors than in Blg-Cre tumors and part of the broad basal program the paper reports.

entities.name: Wfdc18
entities.description: Mouse secretory luminal marker with no clean human ortholog, higher in Blg-Cre than Wap-Cre tumors and also expressed by lactocytes in the developmental atlas.

entities.name: KRT8
entities.description: Luminal keratin, higher in Blg-Cre tumors, and used in both immunofluorescence and CODEX to identify luminal and hybrid cells.

entities.name: ESR1
entities.description: Estrogen receptor, absent from tumors in both models, which is part of what establishes them as triple-negative, and a marker of hormone-sensing luminal cells.

entities.name: SETBP1
entities.description: One of three genes expressed more highly in Wap-Cre than Blg-Cre tumors, offering a concrete gene-level distinction between the two models.

entities.name: ETV5
entities.description: Transcription factor expressed more highly in Wap-Cre than Blg-Cre tumors.

entities.name: Hormone receptor signaling
entities.description: The non-genetic route the introduction proposes for BRCA1 tissue specificity, since BRCA1 targets hormone receptors for degradation and hormone receptors direct epithelial differentiation; proposed but not tested in this paper.

entities.name: Lineage-restricted fat pad transplantation
entities.description: Implantation of sorted basal or luminal cells from matched pre-tumor mutant donors into cleared mammary fat pads of NSG mice, the only experiment here that isolates cell of origin from Cre driver and allele differences.

entities.name: CopyKAT copy-number inference
entities.description: Inference of chromosomal gains and losses from single-cell expression, used to call cells aneuploid and so transformed, and the sole basis for the claim that only luminal cells transform in the Blg-Cre model.

entities.name: MAESTER single-cell genotyping
entities.description: Targeted amplification of the Trp53 transcript from barcoded single-cell cDNA, used because Brca1 is too large for multiplexed PCR, to read which cell types actually carry the recombined allele.

entities.name: CODEX spatial proteomics
entities.description: Cyclic imaging of a DNA-barcoded antibody panel on intact tissue, used to locate smooth muscle actin negative basal cells and proliferation within mutant glands.

entities.name: TNBCtype classifier
entities.description: The Vanderbilt centroid-correlation classifier that assigns a bulk or pseudo-bulk expression profile to one of the four TNBC subtypes, applied here to mouse tumors via MGI ortholog mapping.

entities.name: Mouse mammary developmental atlas (GEO GSE164017)
entities.description: Public reference spanning fetal through involution stages, re-annotated here into eight epithelial states, which is what defines the fetal basal state the tumor cells resemble.

entities.name: Human Breast Cell Atlas (GEO GSE235326)
entities.description: Public human reference with one major basal-myoepithelial population and seven secretory luminal subpopulations, used for the cross-species mapping of the cell of origin.

entities.name: BGFR TNBC cohort
entities.description: Basser-Gray Foundation Repository cohort of 51 TNBC patients, 35 BRCA1 carriers and 16 non-carriers with 34 newly reported, curated by the Nathanson laboratory and with no public accession in the retrievable text.

entities.name: TCGA-BRCA TNBC cohort
entities.description: Public cohort of 132 TNBC patients including 12 BRCA1 carriers, accessed through UCSC Xena, used both to derive the human mesenchymal signature and to validate subtype frequencies.

relations.evidence: Pathogenic germline BRCA1 variants carry a cumulative breast cancer risk of up to 72 percent by age 80, with triple-negative disease the characteristic presentation.
BRCA1 targets hormone receptors for degradation through its E3 ubiquitin ligase domain, and hormone receptors direct epithelial differentiation.
Both mouse models combine Brca1 deletion with p53 loss, since TP53 is the most common co-mutation in BRCA1 breast cancer.

Blg-Cre tumors, which arise from secretory luminal cells, were assigned the basal-like 1 subtype by pseudo-bulk classification and their aneuploid pre-malignant cells were already basal-like 1 enriched.

5 of 7 Wap-Cre tumors classified as mesenchymal, their pre-malignant aneuploid cells leaned basal-myoepithelial and mesenchymal-like, and only transplanted basal cells reproduced the basal-containing composition of spontaneous tumors.

Pre-tumor aneuploid cells are mostly mature basal-myoepithelial and secretory luminal cells with few basal or hybrid cells, which argues that the fetal-like basal state is generated by de-differentiation rather than expanded from a residual population.
Tumor basal-myoepithelial cells and the fetal-like basal state do not express Acta2, and the same loss is seen as smooth muscle actin negative basal cells in spatial imaging.
Loss of myoepithelial marker expression extends from the basal to the hybrid state in both mouse models.
Basal-myoepithelial cells were annotated by Krt14 together with Acta2 in the single-cell atlas, and KRT14 defines basal cells in the imaging panel.
TP63 was co-stained with KRT14 to score whether transplant-derived tumors contained basal cells.
Secretory luminal cells were annotated by Wfdc18 together with Kit.
Luminal hormone-sensing cells were annotated by Esr1 together with Pgr.
Wap-Cre mesenchymal tumors carried higher Krt5 and Trp63 than Blg-Cre tumors, and both Wap-Cre and human mesenchymal tumors showed higher basal gene expression.
Blg-Cre basal-like 1 tumors carried higher Wfdc18, Krt8 and Ehf than Wap-Cre tumors.
Setbp1 was expressed more highly in Wap-Cre tumors than in Blg-Cre tumors.
Etv5 was expressed more highly in Wap-Cre tumors than in Blg-Cre tumors.

The aneuploid bridging population made up about 10 percent of epithelial cells in mutant glands against under 1 percent in wild-type glands, and abnormal basal cells localized to hyperbranched hyperplastic regions.
The basal layer of hyperplastic hyperbranched regions lacked smooth muscle actin, matching the fetal-like basal state, while normal-looking regions of the same gland did not differ from wild-type.

Single-cell genotyping of the recombined Trp53 transcript found recombined alleles in basal-myoepithelial as well as secretory luminal cells of mutant Wap-Cre glands, so Wap-Cre activity is not confined to the luminal compartment.

Human basal-myoepithelial cells scored highest for the mesenchymal signature and LumSec-myo also classified as mesenchymal-like, so both are candidate human counterparts of the Wap-Cre cell of origin, though the mouse cells mapping to them do not express Acta2.
Transcriptome profiling divides TNBC into basal-like 1, basal-like 2, mesenchymal and luminal androgen receptor subtypes that differ in prognosis and drug response.
BRCA1 carriers in the BGFR and TCGA cohorts developed all four TNBC subtypes at roughly the same proportions as patients with sporadic TNBC, so no single subtype defines carrier disease.
Subtypes were assigned by highest centroid correlation using the web-based Vanderbilt TNBCtype classifier, with mouse pseudo-bulk profiles mapped to human genes through the MGI Homology Suite.
Cells were called aneuploid, and therefore transformed, by CopyKAT inference of chromosomal gains and losses from expression, against FACS-sorted wild-type epithelium as the normal baseline.

Smooth muscle actin negative basal cells were identified in intact tissue by cyclic multiplexed antibody imaging, though the panel cannot separate a developmental fetal basal cell from a Bmyo cell that lost its markers.
Basal and luminal fractions sorted from matched pre-tumor mutant donors were implanted into cleared fat pads, and only basal-derived tumors contained KRT14 positive TP63 positive cells.
The fetal basal state was defined by re-annotating the public mouse mammary developmental atlas into eight epithelial states, and tumor cells were assigned to it by co-embedding.
LumSec-myo is one of seven secretory luminal subpopulations in the reprocessed Human Breast Cell Atlas, and it bridges basal and luminal cells in the integrated embedding.
The human mesenchymal signature was scored across the 51-patient BGFR cohort, where the Wap-Cre epithelial signature was highest in mesenchymal tumors at P = 0.0081.
The human mesenchymal signature was derived from TCGA basal-like TNBC and the Wap-Cre signature scored highest in mesenchymal tumors there at P = 0.0068.
The mammary epithelium is a bilayer of an outer basal-myoepithelial layer and an inner luminal layer containing secretory and hormone-sensing cells.
Wild-type glands showed the expected outer basal-myoepithelial and inner luminal layers in multiplexed imaging.
The Trp53 transcript was amplified from barcoded single-cell cDNA, because Brca1 is too large for multiplexed PCR, to read the recombined allele per cell.

Large Wap-Cre tumors contained large hybrid, proliferating luminal and secretory luminal populations while retaining the mesenchymal-like program, and metastases enriched for luminal states kept the same subtype distribution.

Both transplanted basal and luminal fractions produced KRT8 positive luminal cells and hybrid cells, so hybrid cells arise from either compartment, while only basal-derived tumors also contained basal cells.
The Blg-Cre model combines floxed Brca1 exons 21 to 23 with p53 heterozygosity, so p53 loss is part of this model as it is of the Wap-Cre model.
